data.title: 3M, DuPont must face Connecticut firefighters' lawsuit over 'forever chemicals'
data.description:
3M, DuPont must face Connecticut firefighters' lawsuit over 'forever chemicals'

By Jonathan Stempel
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 7:40 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The logo of 3M is seen at the 3M Tilloy plant in Tilloy-Lez-Cambrai

1 of 2
The logo of 3M is seen at the 3M Tilloy plant in Tilloy-Lez-Cambrai, France, August 18, 2019. REUTERS/Pascal Rossignol

By Jonathan Stempel

Sept 15 (Reuters) - A federal judge on Tuesday said more than 20 defendants including 3M, DuPont and Honeywell must face claims by Connecticut firefighters ‌who said their protective gear was contaminated by toxic "forever chemicals" that increased their ‌risk of cancer.

Lawyers for 13 firefighter union organizations and 12 individual firefighters said "turnout gear" that shields against extreme heat ​and flames leached the chemicals through absorption into skin, ingestion and inhalation. They have called the proposed class action the first to exclusively target firefighter gear containing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

U.S. District Judge Alvin Thompson in Hartford, Connecticut, said the unions had "organizational" standing to seek damages, and ‌firefighters could seek damages and medical ⁠monitoring even if they had no outward symptoms of cancer and other diseases.

The judge also said the plaintiffs sufficiently alleged that 3M, one ⁠of the largest manufacturers of PFAS, owed a duty to warn about the risks and committed negligence.

PFAS in firefighters' protective gear included 3M's Scotchlite reflective material and DuPont's Kevlar, while Honeywell manufactured turnout ​gear, according ​to the complaint. Some DuPont liabilities now belong ​to two spinoffs, Chemours and Corteva.

Lawyers ‌for 3M, DuPont, Chemours, Corteva and Honeywell did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Jennifer Sclar, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said the decision was significant because it found that prolonged exposure to PFAS from turnout gear justified legal standing.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

PFAS WIDELY USED

In seeking dismissals, 3M said there were no plausible claims tying Scotchlite to firefighters' gear, while other defendants said there ‌was no allegation that the gear "failed to serve its ​function of protecting firefighters from the hazards of fighting ​fires."

The lawsuit began in June 2024.

PFAS are ​found in hundreds of consumer and commercial products including cosmetics, non-stick pans ‌and stain-resistant clothing.

They are known as "forever chemicals" ​because they do not ​break down easily in the human body or environment. PFAS have also been linked to higher cholesterol, low birth weight and reduced antibody response to vaccines.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In 2023, DuPont, ​3M and two other companies ‌reached more than $11 billion in settlements to resolve claims that firefighting foam and other ​products containing their PFAS polluted drinking water. None admitted wrongdoing.

(Reporting by Jonathan ​Stempel in New York; Editing by Bill Berkrot)

data.title: Trump says Kennedy Center to close after judge bars name change
data.description:
Trump says Kennedy Center to close after judge bars name change

Danny KEMP and Daniel STUBLEN
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 7:36 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

US President Donald Trump said Tuesday that the Kennedy Center will close down -- possibly for good -- after a judge ruled his name cannot be added onto the famed arts institution's exterior.

Trump said the Washington cultural venue's trustees voted to shut down for what it is says are vital emergency renovations, and that it won't reopen unless the judgment is overruled.

"The Board of The Kennedy Center today agreed, almost unanimously, to close the Building for Safety reasons, and so that it can begin the process of Reconstruction," Trump said in a post on his Truth Social network.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump said it would close immediately but said the "very large and complex" renovations cannot begin until a higher court rules on whether it can be renamed after himself.

"If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place."

Shortly after beginning his second term, Republican Trump installed himself as chairman of the center, which is named in honor of late president John F. Kennedy, a Democrat who championed civil rights before he was assassinated in 1963.

The board voted in December to call it the "Trump-Kennedy" Center.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The renaming is one of several projects aimed at stamping Trump's brand on the US capital during his second term, including a triumphal arch and a $400-million ballroom at the White House.

US federal judge Christopher Cooper previously ordered Trump's name removed from the center's exterior and overturned the board's decision to rename the institution.

Workers removed Trump's name from the building in June, but scaffolding and tarps have remained ever since.

- Demolition threat -

Cooper ruled on Tuesday that Trump's name cannot be added back, rebuking the center for trying to circumvent an earlier order.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Simply put," wrote Cooper in his decision, the board "cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing."

The ruling came as the board met to consider a shutdown of the center, citing citing fiscal and safety concerns.

Last month, the board moved forward with a plan to add a new signage on the building that would read "renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump."

Cooper on Tuesday said that plan was in violation of his previous ruling.

Trump and his chosen leaders of the Kennedy Center have argued that its main building, which was constructed in the 1960s, is in a state of dangerous disrepair.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

As evidence of the safety problems, the president pointed to a recent incident in which a piece of the ceiling tumbled to the ground following a storm.

"If the Building were open, innocent people would have been killed," he wrote in a post on Truth Social before the judge's ruling.

"The Board of The Kennedy Center has strongly voted to save it, and they know I'm the only one who can do so, because I have the ability to raise the money, and the ability to construct -- that few others have," Trump said.

Last month, as part of court proceedings, the Trump administration warned that the center may need to be demolished, if its plans to renovate the building were blocked.

A host of artists canceled concerts at the venue in response to Trump's takeover, while US media has reported that Kennedy Center ticket sales have plummeted.

data.title: Attorney General Blanche says FBI has new information on man who shot Trump
data.description:
Attorney General Blanche says FBI has new information on man who shot Trump

By Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff and Nandita Bose
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 7:34 pm UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche holds a press conference at the White House

1 of 3
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche holds a press conference in the Rose Garden at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 15, 2026. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst

By Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff and Nandita Bose

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Tuesday that the ‌FBI had discovered new information regarding the shooter who ‌attempted to assassinate Donald Trump during a campaign event in Butler, Pennsylvania, in 2024.

"It ​is new information about the shooter and about his background, about his history and that stuff that we didn't know before," Blanche told reporters during a White House press conference, without elaborating.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The comments ‌from Blanche came hours ⁠after Trump claimed on social media that new information was found about the assassination attempt and alleged ⁠without evidence that it was really a "Democrat Plot, to get me out of the Election."

Investigations into the shooting have found the shooter acted ​alone ​and produced no evidence Democrats had ​anything to do with ‌the shooting.

Trump added that ex-FBI Director Christopher Wray, whom Trump appointed in his first term but later grew to hate, "should pay a price" for how the department responded to the assassination attempt "and certainly for the things he said."

Blanche, who was Trump's personal lawyer at ‌the time of the assassination attempt, ​said during the briefing that he ​was with Trump as the ​investigation into the shooting was playing out, trying to ‌ascertain what happened.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"His frustration and concern ​about what the ​former director was doing is something that is not new," Blanche said.

The Justice Department and FBI did not immediately ​respond to a request ‌for comment. Wray could not be reached for comment.

(Reporting ​by Nandita Bose and Gram Slattery; editing by Costas ​Pitas, Michael Learmonth and Cynthia Osterman)

data.title: Melania Gives AI ‘Gifts’ To Elementary Students — Just Days After Frightening AI Warnings
data.description:
Melania Gives AI ‘Gifts’ To Elementary Students — Just Days After Frightening AI Warnings

Paige Skinner
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 7:27 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

First lady Melania Trump visited a North Carolina school on Tuesday to surprise students with AI subscriptions as the Trump administration calls the panic over artificial intelligence a "hoax."

Trump visited Mountain View Elementary School in Jefferson, North Carolina, and announced that as part of her anti-cyberbullying "Be Best" initiative, she would gift 1,500 students in Ashe County subscriptions to the AI learning platform StudyFetch and give some schools Jetson Nano Developer Kits, small computers that run AI models.

"Dream big and use these AI tools to build something never created before," she said Tuesday to the school's students and staff. "Maybe one of you will create the next robot. And if you do, make sure you bring it into the White House to show me."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

The first lady's visit comes just a week after Jacob Coxon, a researcher for Anthropic, announced his resignation from the AI company, saying "the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," and that neither Anthropic nor OpenAI is "acting responsibly."

A few other Anthropic employees responded to Coxon's post on X, amplifying his message and saying there is more than a 10% chance the technology could "kill all humans."

Politics: Melania Trump Strolls In With Humanoid Robot — And Somehow It Gets Weirder From There

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has also sounded the alarm, saying that AI leaders are "not preparing" for the new era.

Even with top tech leaders voicing their concerns, President Donald Trump is not interested in regulating AI.

House Speaker Mike Johnson echoed those claims, saying Tuesday that slowing down the development of AI would only let China win the AI race, which would have "serious national security implications for every American family."

data.title: South Africa intensifies hunt after eight women found dead
data.description:
South Africa intensifies hunt after eight women found dead

Hillary ORINDE and Jeanette CHABALALA
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 7:23 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

South African police are racing to crack the killings of at least eight women whose bodies have been found east of Johannesburg in two months, the latest on Tuesday.

The country has one of the world's highest homicide rates but the discovery of the women's bodies, partially naked and battered, has sparked fresh anxiety and raised fears that a serial killer or group of killers may be operating in the area.

Police said six bodies were recovered in the Ekurhuleni municipality in just one week, with only two of the victims identified so far.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

It remained unclear whether the killings were carried out by a single perpetrator, multiple suspects or copycat criminals, police said.

"The challenge is ahead of us and the deaths of these young women must not be in vain," acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia told reporters after a meeting to discuss the killings.

"We live in a society that is violent, there's a lot of aggression and I hope that we will come to a day when the women of our society are safe," he said, calling it "a terrible scourge".

Gender-based violence is endemic in South Africa, where one in three women experiences physical or sexual violence during her lifetime, according to the United Nations, despite years of government pledges to tackle it.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

One of the victims, 38-year-old Elizabeth Moselakgomo, left her eight-year-old daughter at home to go for a jog and never returned. Her body was found on September 12 behind a hotel, police said.

Her disappearance drew public attention after fellow runners launched a social media campaign to find her, bringing renewed focus to earlier cases and, later, to the discovery of more bodies.

The first victim, a 37-year-old woman, was found naked and bound with cable ties on July 15, police said. A suspect was arrested two days later.

A second woman, 32, was found partially clothed on August 24, while a third was discovered naked and in an advanced state of decomposition on September 10.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

- 'No stone unturned' -

President Cyril Ramaphosa on Tuesday said "no stone will be left unturned" to solve the killings, acknowledging "these incidents are causing fear and uncertainty in our communities, and especially among women".

The killings have drawn condemnation from civil society and sporting bodies as calls grow for action on gender-based violence, which South Africa has declared a national emergency.

Amnesty International South Africa said the discovery of the bodies was "just another horrific reminder that women in South Africa are not safe".

South Africa, a nation of 62 million people, has some of the highest rates of violence against women and children in the world, according to UN Women.

At least 60 people are killed each day in South Africa, many linked to turf battles between gangs involved in drugs and illegal mining.

data.title: US Senate fails to advance sweeping cryptocurrency bill in blow for industry
data.description:
By Hannah Lang

Sept 15 (Reuters) - The U.S. Senate failed to advance ‌comprehensive cryptocurrency legislation on Tuesday ‌in a major blow for digital asset ​companies and Republicans who had championed the bill for months.

The vote effectively put the bill, dubbed the ‌Clarity Act, on ⁠ice, as Congress is set to depart Washington this ⁠month ahead of the November midterm elections in which President Donald ​Trump's fellow ​Republicans are ​fighting to retain ‌control of the House of Representatives and Senate.

The Clarity Act aimed to create a regulatory framework for digital assets, which crypto companies say ‌would put them on ​a more solid ​legal footing. ​The deep-pocketed industry spent hundreds of ‌millions of dollars campaigning ​to ​advance the bill.

(Reporting by Hannah Lang in New York; Additional reporting ​by ‌Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss in New York; Editing ​by Matthew Lewis, Will Dunham ​and Hugh Lawson)

data.title: US Congress Democrats probe Russian oligarch financing of Trump Jr. wedding parties
data.description:
US Congress Democrats probe Russian oligarch financing of Trump Jr. wedding parties

By Richard Cowan and Alexandra Ulmer
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 7:27 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Richard Cowan and Alexandra Ulmer

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Democrats in the U.S. Congress launched an investigation this week into reports that a Russian oligarch paid hundreds ‌of thousands of dollars for the wedding celebrations of President Donald Trump's son ‌earlier this year.

The Democrats' move comes on the heels of an article by ProPublica that Umar Kremlev, a wealthy ​Russian businessman and president of the International Boxing Association, paid for wedding festivities for Donald Trump Jr. in the Bahamas in May.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The report said that Kremlev has close ties to the Russian government.

"Why is a Russian oligarch and friend of Vladimir Putin financially supporting the President's son? What does Umar ‌Kremlev expect in return for ⁠funding this three-day wedding in the Bahamas?" Representative Robert Garcia wrote on Tuesday in a social media post.

Garcia is the senior Democrat on the House ⁠Oversight and Government Reform Committee and is expected to chair the panel if Democrats win a majority in the House of Representatives in November's midterm elections.

A representative for Don Jr declined to comment.

His ​wife, Bettina ​Trump, said in an Instagram post on Monday ​that Kremlev was a friend who ‌had extended an "extraordinarily generous wedding gift," stressing that Kremlev had paid for two after-parties, not the wedding itself.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Kremlev and the IBA did not respond to requests for comment on Tuesday.

The president, who did not attend his son's wedding, said in a statement that he did not know Kremlev and that the wedding controversy was "not a big deal!"

Aides to Republican Representative James Comer of ‌Kentucky, who chairs the committee, did not immediately respond ​to a request for comment.

Garcia and other leading House Democrats ​already have been gearing up for ​probes into Trump, his family and ethics questions that have arisen since ‌the start of the president's second term ​in January 2025.

Senate Democratic Leader ​Chuck Schumer of New York on Tuesday called the wedding arrangement "so corrupt, so venal, so endangering our national security."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In a speech to the Senate, Schumer added, "You're dealing with ​a Russian oligarch, not just ‌a cousin who's giving you a gift...sometimes a wedding gift is a bribe from ​a foreign autocrat."

(Reporting by Richard Cowan and Alexandra Ulmer; additional reporting by Nandita ​Bose; Editing by Michael Learmonth and Cynthia Osterman)

data.title: US attorney general says probes handled by ex-prosecutor DiGenova will continue
data.description:
US attorney general says probes handled by ex-prosecutor DiGenova will continue

Reuters
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 7:05 pm UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche holds a press conference at the White House

1 of 4
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks during a press conference in the Rose Garden at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 15, 2026. REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Tuesday that any probes that ‌former federal prosecutor Joseph DiGenova had been handling ‌would continue.

DiGenova, who oversaw a wide-ranging probe into past investigations of ​President Donald Trump, resigned last week.

"I very much appreciate the work that he did for us and for the administration," Blanche told reporters at the White house. "Any investigations ‌that he's working ⁠on, of course, continue like they do, like any investigation does when somebody leaves, ⁠and we're not going to slow down just because somebody leaves."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

DiGenova joined the Justice Department in April to take ​over the ​Florida-based investigation that has ​been scrutinizing several of ‌Trump's foes and has sought to establish that the president was the victim of a long-running criminal conspiracy.

The investigation has examined the 2017 U.S. intelligence finding that Russia sought to boost Trump's first presidential campaign in ‌2016, as well as more ​recent investigations by former Special ​Counsel Jack Smith ​that probed Trump's retention of classified documents ‌at his Mar-a-Lago resort and ​his attempts to ​overturn his 2020 election defeat. The investigation has so far not resulted in any criminal charges.

DiGenova, ​a Trump ally, ‌did not provide a reason for his resignation.

(Reporting ​by Nandita Bose and Doina ChiacuEditing by ​David Ljunggren and Caitlin Webber)

data.title: Israeli strikes in Gaza kill three people, medics say
data.description:
Israeli strikes in Gaza kill three people, medics say

Reuters
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 7:03 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Funeral of Palestinian Raafat Zamar, who was killed in an Israeli strike on on his tent on Monday, according to medics, in Khan Younis

1 of 3
A woman mourns during the funeral of Palestinian Raafat Zamar, who was killed in an Israeli strike on his tent on Monday, according to medics, in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, September 15, 2026. REUTERS/Haseeb Alwazeer

CAIRO/GAZA, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Israeli airstrikes killed at least three Palestinians in the northern Gaza Strip on Tuesday, including a patient at a healthcare center, medics said.

Israeli airstrikes on a vehicle ‌killed at least two Palestinians, one a child, and wounded seven others in the northern Gaza Strip ‌neighbourhood of Sheikh Radwan, according to medics.

The Israeli military said it had struck a militant in the area, without elaborating.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Witnesses said some of ​the casualties resulted from a second strike near a group of people who had rushed to aid the initial victims. A video, which Reuters did not immediately verify, showed a missile exploding near at least five men.

In a separate incident, British health charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said on Tuesday that a patient was killed at a health ‌center it supports in northern Gaza's Jabalia.

The ⁠organization said the patient was shot by an Israeli military quadcopter drone. There was no immediate Israeli comment.

Palestinians earlier held funerals in Gaza for two people who were killed ⁠by Israeli strikes a day ago, Ahmed Al-Batsh and

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Rafat Zummar.

Batsh was a local Hamas commander, according to Hamas sources and the Israeli military. Medics said Batsh died in an attack on his vehicle in the northern Gaza Strip.

The Israeli military ​said in ​separate statements that it had killed both men, and it ​described Zummar also as a Hamas commander. ‌Hamas didn't immediately comment on Zummar's affiliation.

Relatives and friends honored Batsh's body draped in a white shroud and a Hamas green flag at Gaza City's Al Shifa Hospital. An M16 assault rifle was placed on top of the body.

"Israel thinks... it will eliminate the resistance and the spirit of jihad (devotion) within us," said Khalil Al-Batsh, a relative of the dead Hamas militant.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I tell them that this cowardly operation only strengthens our people's determination to continue on ‌this path," he told Reuters at the funeral.

An October 2025, ​U.S.-backed, ceasefire halted large-scale fighting in Gaza, but it has not ​ended Israeli strikes and there has been little ​progress on steps towards permanent peace.

Hamas accuses Israel of violating the ceasefire and undermining efforts ‌to implement U.S. President Donald Trump's broader plan ​to end the Gaza conflict, ​which includes the Israeli withdrawal from the strip and the disarmament of Hamas.

Israel says Hamas has been violating the deal.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

More than 1,300 Palestinians, mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took ​effect, according to the territory's health ‌officials, while the Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed.

Hamas does not usually disclose ​information about fatalities among its fighters.

(Reporting by Nidal al-Mughrabi and Dawoud Abu Alkas and Haseeb Alwazir ​in Gaza; Editing by Alexandra Hudson and Cynthia Osterman)
